stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Delia Marsh's 2011 novel The Quiet Needle. Ines, a newly hired technician, is spending her first night at a remote seismic monitoring station.

Ines had always pictured seismology as a dull business of numbers, and she had taken the station job mostly for the salary. Yet when the recording drum began to turn and the needle traced the faint tremors of a quake hundreds of miles away, she found she could not look away. She pulled her chair closer. Each small flicker of ink seemed to her a message from deep inside the earth, and she stayed awake until dawn, waiting for the next one.
choices: To explain how the station's instruments record earthquakes that occur far away
To portray Ines's growing fascination with work she had expected to find dull
To show Ines's regret at having accepted a job only for the salary it paid
To reveal how Ines first became interested in studying earthquakes as a child
explanation: The setup line tells you Ines is the focus. The excerpt opens with what she used to believe (seismology is dull), then turns on 'Yet': she can't look away, pulls her chair closer, and stays up until dawn. Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her becoming fascinated by work she expected to be boring, and that is what B says.

A.why: You picked a choice about the drum and needle, which are incidental details. The excerpt never explains how the instruments work. It uses them to show how Ines reacts. This is the content trap: the choice describes things in the text and ignores what the excerpt is doing.

C.why: You went with the salary detail and missed the turn at 'Yet.' Ines does not regret taking the job. She is so absorbed that she stays awake until dawn, which is the opposite of regret.

D.why: You added a detail the text never gives. The excerpt says nothing about Ines's childhood. In fact, it says she used to think seismology was dull. Stick to what the excerpt as a whole conveys.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Varga's 1998 poem "For the Bridge Builders."

They say the river does not remember who tamed it,
that no plaque will ever carry your names.
But you who sink the pilings in the cold brown current,
who bolt the girders while the wind leans hard,
look up: each morning thousands cross the water
on the strength of what your hands have set.
Build on. The far bank is waiting,
and the span you raise will hold for years.
choices: To warn the bridge builders about the dangers of working above a river in high winds
To describe the materials and methods used to construct a bridge across a river
To criticize the public for failing to learn the names of the people who build bridges
To encourage the bridge builders by affirming the lasting value of their labor
explanation: The poem speaks to the builders ('you who sink the pilings'). It first states a discouraging view, that nobody will remember them, and then corrects it with 'But.' After that it points to the thousands who cross the bridge every day and urges the builders to 'Build on' because their span 'will hold for years.' The tone is encouraging, so D is correct.

A.why: You reversed the poem's tone. The wind and cold current show how hard the work is, but the poem never warns the builders. It cheers them on with 'Build on.' Encouraging is not the same as warning.

B.why: You noticed the pilings and girders and took them to be the point. The poem mentions these details only to honor the people doing the work. It never explains how a bridge is built.

C.why: You read too much into the line about no plaque. The poem mentions that the builders go unnamed only so it can answer that worry. It never blames the public. The speaker's attention stays on the builders the whole time.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Hal Bergstrom's 2004 memoir Forty Acres East. A soil scientist has persuaded the narrator's father to let her test a new planting method on one strip of the family's farm.

My father had farmed the same way for thirty years and trusted nothing that came out of a university. When the scientist marked off her strip of clover-covered rows, he stood at the fence with his arms folded and said nothing. But all that summer I caught him walking out to that strip at dusk, crouching to press the dark soil between his fingers, then glancing back at his own dry rows. By August he had stopped pretending not to care.
choices: To portray the father's quiet, growing interest in a method he had first distrusted
To convey the narrator's own wish to become a soil scientist after that summer
To explain why the clover method produced richer soil than the father's method
To show the father's open hostility toward the scientist throughout the summer
explanation: Even though the narrator tells the story, the excerpt is about the father. He starts out distrustful, with folded arms and nothing to say. After 'But,' he keeps going back to the test strip to feel the soil, and by August he has 'stopped pretending not to care.' A names the right person and the right change.

B.why: You shifted the focus from the father to the narrator and added a wish the text never mentions. The narrator only watches. Nothing in the excerpt says the narrator wants a career in soil science.

C.why: You noticed the 'dark soil' next to the 'dry rows' and assumed the excerpt is about the science. It never says why the clover method works. That contrast is there to show the father's reaction.

D.why: You stopped reading after the folded arms. The father is silent at the start, not openly hostile, and over the summer he softens. 'Throughout the summer' contradicts the change the excerpt shows.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Nandakumar's 2015 novel The Piece Rate. Jonah works at a garment factory where pay is about to change from an hourly wage to a set amount for each finished shirt.

The foreman announced the change as though it were a gift: from now on, every shirt would earn its own wage. Jonah, however, did the arithmetic in his head and felt his stomach tighten. He was careful, not fast, and he knew it. Around him, the younger workers were already grinning and flexing their fingers. Jonah bent over his machine and tried to make his hands move quicker, but every crooked seam he had to tear out seemed to cost him more than thread.
choices: To portray the younger workers' excitement about earning more under the new system
To explain why the factory's owners decided to change how the workers would be paid
To convey Jonah's anxiety that the new pay system will leave him worse off
To show Jonah's relief that his careful work will finally be properly rewarded
explanation: The setup line names Jonah as the focus. The foreman presents the change as a gift, and 'however' turns to Jonah's reaction: his stomach tightens, he knows he is slow, and every mistake now 'cost him more than thread.' The excerpt as a whole conveys his worry that pay per shirt will hurt him, so C is correct.

A.why: You chose a character who is in the excerpt but is not its focus. The grinning younger workers get one sentence, and they are there to contrast with Jonah. The excerpt is about his feelings, not theirs.

B.why: You chose a detail the text never gives. The excerpt says nothing about why the owners changed the pay system. It only shows how Jonah reacts to the change.

D.why: You reversed Jonah's feeling. Being careful instead of fast is exactly why he expects to lose under the new system, so he is anxious, not relieved.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Clara Wendell's 1919 novel The Gauge-Keeper. Ada has just been hired to record the daily water level of the river near her family's farm.

Each morning Ada walked down to the painted post at the river's edge and read the number the water touched. Her father called it dull work, but to Ada it was nothing of the kind. She had begun to notice how the river rose a finger's width two days after rain fell in the hills, and how it slackened in the summer heat. Writing the figures into the ledger, she felt she was learning a language the river had been speaking all along.
choices: To convey Ada's father's disapproval of the work his daughter has taken on
To suggest that Ada finds the daily task tedious and wishes to give it up
To portray Ada's growing fascination with the river as she records its levels
To describe how Ada learned to predict floods before they reached the farm
explanation: The setup line tells you Ada is the focus. Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her noticing patterns in the river: it rises after rain in the hills and slackens in the heat. It ends with her feeling that she is learning the river's language. That is growing fascination, and choice C names both the right person and the right feeling.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ada to her father. His remark that the work is dull comes up once, and only so the text can show that Ada feels the opposite. The excerpt is about her experience, not his opinion.

B.why: You took the father's word "dull" as Ada's own view. The text says the work was "nothing of the kind" to her, and nothing suggests she wants to quit.

D.why: You added a detail the text never gives. Ada notices how the water level changes after rain, but the excerpt never says she predicts floods or protects the farm.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Lena Okafor's 2019 novel *The Cold Dome*. Teodora, a young astronomer, is starting her first night of work at a mountain observatory.

For weeks Teodora had told everyone the night would be routine: calibrate the telescope, log the data, sleep. But when the dome slid open and the cold sky poured in, she found her hands shaking on the controls. She had studied these stars since childhood, yet she had never felt so close to them.
choices: To explain the steps an astronomer follows to calibrate a telescope
To convey Teodora's unexpectedly strong emotion at the start of her work
To show that Teodora's colleagues doubted she was ready for the job
To portray Teodora's disappointment that the night was only routine
explanation: The setup puts the focus on Teodora. The excerpt says she expected a routine night, and then the word 'But' turns it around: her hands shake and she feels closer to the stars than ever before. The excerpt as a whole conveys a strong emotion she did not expect, which is what B says.

A.why: You picked a detail. Calibration comes up only as part of what Teodora expected, and the text never explains how it is done. That is content, not the excerpt's purpose.

C.why: You added people the text never mentions. Teodora told 'everyone' her plans, but no colleague doubts her anywhere in the excerpt.

D.why: You reversed the turn in the excerpt. The night is not routine. It moves her deeply, and nothing suggests she is disappointed.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Marisol Ekwueme's 2008 poem "To the One Who Draws the District." The speaker addresses a city planner.

Planner, when you draw the new streets,
leave sidewalks wide enough for two to walk
and talk without one stepping into traffic.
Leave a bench where the bus is slow to come.
The council will ask for speed and parking;
give them some, but keep a square of shade
where a grandmother can rest. You can do this.
Your lines will outlast every meeting.
choices: To warn the planner that the council will reject any design with shade
To lament that the city has already lost its benches and shaded squares
To encourage the planner to design streets around people's daily lives
To describe how the city's current street layout was first developed
explanation: The poem is spoken to the planner. It asks for wide sidewalks, a bench, and shade for people to rest in, and it ends with 'You can do this.' The poem as a whole encourages the planner to design for how people actually live, which is what C says.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The council asks for speed and parking, but the speaker says to 'give them some' and keep the shade too. The poem is hopeful and is not a warning about rejection.

B.why: You turned a hopeful poem into a lament. The streets are 'new' and haven't been built, so the poem never says anything has been lost.

D.why: You chose a history the poem never gives. It looks ahead to a district that hasn't been drawn yet. It says nothing about how the current layout came to be.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Samuel Arce's 2015 memoir *Load and Span*. Arce, a civil engineer, has brought his father to see the first bridge Arce designed.

I had expected my father, who had poured concrete for forty years, to inspect every joint. Instead, he walked to the middle of the span and stood there, saying nothing, while trucks rumbled past. When he finally turned back, he only rested his hand on the railing. I understood then that he had already approved of it, and of me.
choices: To show the father's regret about his own long career pouring concrete
To describe the narrator's worry that the bridge's joints contained flaws
To explain how passing trucks are used to test the strength of a bridge
To convey the narrator's realization that his father's silence meant approval
explanation: The narrator expects a strict inspection. What he gets instead is silence and a hand on the railing, and the last sentence says what he takes from it: 'he had already approved of it, and of me.' The excerpt builds to the narrator's realization, which is what D says.

A.why: You read a feeling into the father that the text never gives him. His forty years of work are mentioned, but nothing suggests he regrets them.

B.why: You misread the opening. The narrator expected his father to inspect the joints. He never says he feared they were flawed, and the excerpt ends with approval, not worry.

C.why: You picked a background detail. The trucks only set the scene while the father stands on the bridge. The excerpt is not about how bridges are tested.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Priya Venkataraman's 2021 novel *Cover Crop*. Ruth, a soil scientist, has returned to her family's farm to run field trials.

Ruth's test plots were thriving: the clover she had sown between the corn rows had held the soil through two hard storms, and even her uncle admitted the results were good. Yet each evening she caught herself looking at the fields her grandfather had plowed bare every spring, unsure whether she was improving the farm or erasing him from it.
choices: To portray Ruth's mixed feelings about changing how her family has farmed
To portray the uncle's reluctant pride in his niece's scientific research
To explain why clover keeps soil in place during heavy storms
To convey Ruth's regret that her test plots had failed to succeed
explanation: The setup puts the focus on Ruth. Her new method works, but the word 'Yet' brings in her doubt: she can't tell whether she is improving the farm or erasing her grandfather's way of farming it. The excerpt as a whole shows that she feels torn, which is what A says.

B.why: You picked the right family but the wrong person. The uncle appears in one clause, and the excerpt is about what Ruth feels, not what he feels.

C.why: You described the content, not the purpose. The clover detail sets up Ruth's success, but the text never explains why it holds soil in place, and the excerpt is about her inner conflict.

D.why: You reversed a stated fact. The plots are 'thriving,' so Ruth's doubt comes from success, not failure.
